introduction: On this Sunday, Solomon asks God not for riches or long life but for an understanding heart. In the Gospel, Jesus compares the Kingdom of Heaven to a treasure hidden in a field and a pearl of great price, for which a person sells everything with joy. Paul tells us that all things work together for good for those who love God. Let us seek the Kingdom above all else.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God's law is more precious than gold. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may treasure the Kingdom of God above all earthly goods. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who govern and those who judge: that God may give them wise and understanding hearts. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are searching for meaning: that they may find the treasure of the Kingdom. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are suffering: that they may trust that God works all things together for good. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may let go of whatever keeps us from Christ, with joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you are the treasure beyond all price. Give us understanding hearts, and the joy to choose your Kingdom above everything else. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The pearl of great price
reflection.body:
Young Solomon has just become king, and God appears to him in a dream: "Ask for what I should give you." Solomon could have asked for anything. He knows he is inexperienced: "I am just a little child." So he asks for "an understanding heart to judge your people, that I may discern between good and evil." God is pleased, and gives him "a wise and understanding heart." Solomon chose what truly matters.

In the Gospel, Jesus tells two short parables about the same choice. "Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field." Then: a merchant searching for fine pearls finds "one pearl of great price," and "he went and sold all that he had and bought it."

In the first parable, the man stumbles on the treasure by surprise. In the second, the merchant has been searching. Some people find God unexpectedly; others after a long search. But in both cases, the discovery is so precious that everything else seems small by comparison. Notice the words "In his joy." Giving up other things for the Kingdom is not a grim sacrifice but a joyful exchange.

Jesus adds a third image, a net that gathers fish of every kind, to be sorted at the end. And he ends with the scribe who brings out of his treasure "new and old things," the wisdom of the Old Testament and the new life of the Gospel.

Paul gives us a great promise: "We know that all things work together for good for those who love God." Even what seems like loss can serve God's purpose.

This week, ask yourself: what is my treasure? What would I give anything for? Ask God, like Solomon, for an understanding heart. And let go of one thing that competes with him in your life.
